title: Λήθης Φάρμακον
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Helen slips into the wine a drug from Egypt that banishes grief, then tells of Odysseus's boldest exploit at Troy: disguised as a beaten, ragged beggar, he slipped into the enemy city, recognized only by her, and swore her to silence until he returned to the ships with news of the Trojans' plans. Menelaus caps her story with his own, of the wooden horse: how Helen, prompted by a god who favored Troy, circled the hollow ambush three times, calling out each hidden Achaean by name in his own wife's voice, and how only Odysseus's iron restraint — a hand clamped over Antiklos's mouth — kept the ambush from being betrayed. Telemachus, still grieving, asks only to go to bed; the household settles for the night. At dawn Menelaus rises, arms himself, and asks Telemachus his errand; Telemachus explains that his house is being devoured by his mother's suitors and begs, almost in the very words he used to Nestor, for any word of his father — a plea the part leaves unfinished.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησ’ Ἑλένη Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα·
sentences.tr: enth’ aut’ all’ enoēs’ Helenē Dios ekgegauia·
sentences.l: Then again another thing devised Helen, sprung of Zeus;
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, Helen, the daughter sprung from Zeus, thought of something else;
sentences.n: ἐνόησ’ is ἐνόησε, the aorist of νοέω ’perceive, devise’, and it IS augmented: the initial ἐ- is the augment and stands in plain sight. What is elided is a different vowel — the verb’s own final -ε, dropped before the following vowel-initial Ἑλένη (whose Ἑ- itself carries a rough, not smooth, breathing). This line echoes the fixed formula ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη, with Ἑλένη Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα, ’Helen, sprung of Zeus’, standing in for Athena; ἐκγεγαυῖα, a perfect participle of ἐκγίγνομαι, follows the wording already fixed for Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ εἰς οἶνον βάλε φάρμακον, ἔνθεν ἔπινον,
νηπενθές τ’ ἄχολόν τε, κακῶν ἐπίληθον ἁπάντων.
sentences.tr:
autik’ ar’ eis oinon bale pharmakon, enthen epinon,
nēpenthes t’ acholon te, kakōn epilēthon hapantōn.
sentences.l:
At once then into the wine she threw a drug, from which they drank,
grief-easing and anger-easing, a forgetting of all ills.
sentences.i: At once she threw into the wine they were drinking a drug that eased grief and eased anger, bringing forgetfulness of every trouble.
sentences.n: βάλε is the unaugmented second (thematic) aorist of βάλλω, on the bare stem βαλ-: Attic ἔβαλε simply prefixes the augment to this same stem, so this is exactly the same phenomenon as πάθεν, ἴδεν, φύγον and τέκε — an ordinary past tense without the ἐ- — not an athematic root aorist like ἔβην or the augmented κατέδυ seen below. νηπενθές (νη- privative + πένθος ’grief’) and ἄχολον (ἀ- privative + χόλος ’bile, anger’) describe the drug itself; ἐπίληθον governs the genitive κακῶν ἁπάντων, ’causing forgetfulness of all ills’. This is the poem’s famous nepenthe.

sentences.t:
ὃς τὸ καταβρόξειεν, ἐπὴν κρητῆρι μιγείη,
οὔ κεν ἐφημέριός γε βάλοι κατὰ δάκρυ παρειῶν,
sentences.tr:
hos to katabroxeien, epēn krētēri migeiē,
ou ken ephēmerios ge baloi kata dakry pareiōn,
sentences.l:
whoever should gulp it down, when it had been mixed in the bowl,
would not, for that day at least, let a tear fall down his cheeks,
sentences.i: whoever swallowed it down, once it had been mixed into the bowl, would not shed a single tear the whole day through,
sentences.n: καταβρόξειεν and βάλοι are optatives in a generalizing conditional clause, so the question of augment does not arise for them (the optative never takes one). ἐφημέριος (ἐπί + ἡμέρα) is ’lasting a day, for that day’, a rare word. The sentence that begins here runs five lines to a period at 226; it is cut here, at the comma after παρειῶν, because a period would otherwise run past four lines, and the syntax pauses most strongly at exactly this point, before the two οὐδ’ εἴ clauses begin.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ οἱ κατατεθναίη μήτηρ τε πατήρ τε,
οὐδ’ εἴ οἱ προπάροιθεν ἀδελφεὸν ἢ φίλον υἱὸν
χαλκῷ δηιόῳεν, ὁ δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῷτο.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ei hoi katatethnaiē mētēr te patēr te,
oud’ ei hoi proparoithen adelpheon ē philon huion
chalkōi dēioōien, ho d’ ophthalmoisin horōito.
sentences.l:
not even if his mother and father had died,
not even if before his face his brother or dear son
with the bronze they should slay, and he with his own eyes should see it.
sentences.i: not even if his mother and father had died, not even if before his eyes they killed his brother or dear son with the bronze, and he watched it happen.
sentences.n: κατατεθναίη is a perfect optative of θνῄσκω (reduplicated stem τεθνα-); δηιόῳεν is a present optative of δηϊόω ’slay’ with its contracted -οῖεν artificially stretched to -όῳεν, the same diectasis seen in αἰτιόωνται. ὁρῷτο is a present optative of ὁράω. None of these carries an augment, since the optative mood is never augmented; that issue concerns only indicative past tenses, such as ἐνόησε above.

sentences.t:
τοῖα Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἔχε φάρμακα μητιόεντα,
ἐσθλά, τά οἱ Πολύδαμνα πόρεν, Θῶνος παράκοιτις
Αἰγυπτίη, τῇ πλεῖστα φέρει ζείδωρος ἄρουρα
φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά·
sentences.tr:
toia Dios thygatēr eche pharmaka mētioenta,
esthla, ta hoi Polydamna poren, Thōnos parakoitis
Aigyptiē, tēi pleista pherei zeidōros aroura
pharmaka, polla men esthla memigmena polla de lygra·
sentences.l:
Such cunning drugs the daughter of Zeus possessed,
good ones, which to her Polydamna gave, Thon’s consort,
the Egyptian, whose grain-giving plough-land bears the most
drugs, many good mixed in and many baneful;
sentences.i: Such cunning drugs the daughter of Zeus possessed, good ones that Polydamna, the wife of Thon, had given her, an Egyptian woman whose grain-giving plough-land bears the most drugs of all, many good ones mixed in among many harmful;
sentences.n: Διὸς θυγάτηρ keeps the house rendering ’the daughter of Zeus’ already fixed for Athena, used here of Helen. ζείδωρος ἄρουρα, ’the grain-giving plough-land’, is the phrase already fixed at 3.3, where an ancient alternative reading, ’life-giving’ (from ζάω), is also on record beside the usual ’grain-giving’. μητιόεντα (from μῆτις) describes the drugs as ’cunning, subtly wrought’. Πολύδαμνα and Θῶνος are proper names otherwise unknown to the poem, an Egyptian couple; παράκοιτις is simply ’bedfellow, wife’. πόρεν is an unaugmented second (thematic) aorist (πορ-), the same unaugmented pattern as βάλε above and not, strictly, a root aorist, beside Attic ἔπορεν.

sentences.t:
ἰητρὸς δὲ ἕκαστος ἐπιστάμενος περὶ πάντων
ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
iētros de hekastos epistamenos peri pantōn
anthrōpōn·
sentences.l:
and each physician is skilled beyond all
men;
sentences.i: and every physician there is skilled beyond all other men;
sentences.n: ἐπιστάμενος is a present participle standing with an unexpressed ἐστί (’each physician is skilled’), and it takes the genitive περὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, ’beyond all men’ — the same superiority-with-genitive idiom seen in περὶ… ἐστὶ βροτῶν of Odysseus. The unit ends mid-line 232, at the raised point after ἀνθρώπων, and the rest of that line opens the next unit.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ Παιήονός εἰσι γενέθλης.
sentences.tr: ē gar Paiēonos eisi genethlēs.
sentences.l: for indeed they are of the race of Paieon.
sentences.i: for they are indeed descended from Paieon.
sentences.n: Παιήων (here genitive Παιήονος) is a distinct healing god, older than and separate from Apollo Paean; the two are not the same figure in Homer. γενέθλη is ’stock, race, offspring’. The claim is that Egyptian physicians as a class descend from this god’s line, which explains their famous skill with drugs.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐνέηκε κέλευσέ τε οἰνοχοῆσαι,
ἐξαῦτις μύθοισιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ eneēke keleuse te oinochoēsai,
exautis mythoisin ameibomenē proseeipen·
sentences.l:
But when she had put it in, and bidden them pour the wine,
once more with words, answering, she addressed them:
sentences.i: But when she had put it in and told them to pour the wine, she spoke to them again in these words:
sentences.n: ἐνέηκε, from ἐνίημι, IS augmented, like προσέειπεν just below: the augment ἐ- stands unfused before the root’s own long η (ἐν-έ-ηκε), where Attic contracts the two into a single vowel, ἐνῆκε; κέλευσέ has no augment at all (Attic ἐκέλευσε). προσέειπεν is the uncontracted, still-augmented form of προσεῖπε (προσ-έ-ειπε), left unfused because Homer still feels the lost digamma of the root Ϝεπ-. This line closes the narration of the drug and opens Helen’s second speech of the visit.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς ἠδὲ καὶ οἵδε
ἀνδρῶν ἐσθλῶν παῖδες·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē Menelae diotrephes ēde kai hoide
andrōn esthlōn paides·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’ son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, and you as well,
the sons of noble men;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, and you too, the sons of noble men;
sentences.n: The line adapts the fixed vocative Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν to a different continuation: here Helen also addresses the young men present, οἵδε…παῖδες, ’you here, the sons of noble men’ — Telemachus and Peisistratus. Quotation marks open here (English layers only; Murray prints none) for this new speech, and they are not closed anywhere within this slice.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ θεὸς ἄλλοτε ἄλλῳ
Ζεὺς ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε διδοῖ·
sentences.tr:
atar theos allote allōi
Zeus agathon te kakon te didoi·
sentences.l:
but the god — to one now, to another now —
Zeus gives both good and bad;
sentences.i: but the god Zeus gives good and evil, now to one man, now to another;
sentences.n: ἄλλοτε ἄλλῳ is a distributive idiom, ’at one time to one man, at another to another’, governing διδοῖ, uncontracted for δίδωσι. The claim generalizes what Zeus himself said about mortals blaming the gods for troubles they bring on themselves.

sentences.t: δύναται γὰρ ἅπαντα·
sentences.tr: dynatai gar hapanta·
sentences.l: for he is able to do all things;
sentences.i: for he has power over everything;
sentences.n: δύναται takes ἅπαντα as a bare object (understood as ’to do’), and the half-line simply restates, as a general reason, the claim just made about Zeus’s unlimited power to give both good and bad.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι νῦν δαίνυσθε καθήμενοι ἐν μεγάροισι
καὶ μύθοις τέρπεσθε·
sentences.tr:
ē toi nyn dainysthe kathēmenoi en megaroisi
kai mythois terpesthe·
sentences.l:
Now indeed you feast, sitting in the halls,
and in stories take delight;
sentences.i: Now you are feasting, seated in the halls, and taking your pleasure in stories;
sentences.n: δαίνυσθε and τέρπεσθε are present middle imperatives-cum-descriptions addressed to the diners; μύθοις is an instrumental dative, ’with stories’. μεγάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι(ν) for a single hall, as often.

sentences.t: ἐοικότα γὰρ καταλέξω.
sentences.tr: eoikota gar katalexō.
sentences.l: for fitting things I shall tell in order.
sentences.i: for I will tell a tale that fits the occasion.
sentences.n: ἐοικότα, ’fitting things’, is a neuter plural object of καταλέξω, a future of καταλέγω ’recount in order’, the verb regularly used in this poem for formal storytelling.

sentences.t:
πάντα μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω,
ὅσσοι Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονός εἰσιν ἄεθλοι·
sentences.tr:
panta men ouk an egō mythēsomai oud’ onomēnō,
hossoi Odyssēos talasiphronos eisin aethloi·
sentences.l:
All things I could not tell, nor could I name them all,
as many as are the trials of Odysseus the enduring-minded;
sentences.i: I could not tell everything, nor name it all, all the trials that steadfast Odysseus underwent;
sentences.n: μυθήσομαι and ὀνομήνω are futures (the second an aorist-subjunctive-shaped form with future sense) governed by οὐκ ἄν, a modest disclaimer before the single story Helen will actually tell. ταλασίφρονος keeps the fixed rendering ’enduring-minded’ / ’steadfast’ already used of Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἷον τόδ’ ἔρεξε καὶ ἔτλη καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχετε πήματ’ Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
all’ hoion tod’ erexe kai etlē karteros anēr
dēmōi eni Trōōn, hothi paschete pēmat’ Achaioi.
sentences.l:
But such a thing this strong man did and dared
in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans.
sentences.i: But this strong man did and dared such a thing in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes.
sentences.n: καρτερὸς ἀνήρ, ’the strong man’, is plain and not yet house-fixed. Line 243 is word-for-word the same line already published in odyssey-009 (Telemachus’s plea to Nestor, = 4.243/329); its shipped English, ’in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans’ / ’…in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes’, is reused here verbatim, with only the terminal punctuation changed from comma to period to match this unit’s grammar.

sentences.t:
αὐτόν μιν πληγῇσιν ἀεικελίῃσι δαμάσσας,
σπεῖρα κάκ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι βαλών, οἰκῆι ἐοικώς,
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων κατέδυ πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν·
sentences.tr:
auton min plēgēisin aeikeliēisi damassas,
speira kak’ amph’ ōmoisi balōn, oikēi eoikōs,
andrōn dysmeneōn katedy polin euryaguian·
sentences.i: He disfigured himself with degrading blows and threw foul rags about his shoulders, and looking like a household slave, made his way into the wide-streeted city of his enemies;
sentences.n: δαμάσσας and βαλών are unaugmented aorist participles (no participle ever takes the augment). κατέδυ, by contrast, IS augmented: it is κατά + ἔδυ, the root aorist of δύω ’sink, enter’, with the augment ε- fused inside the tmesis compound; the same verb recurs, still augmented, at 249. εὐρυάγυιαν (εὐρύς + ἄγυια ’street’) is kept distinct from the already-fixed εὐρυόδεια ’wide-wayed’ (of earth), a different noun.

sentences.t:
ἄλλῳ δ’ αὐτὸν φωτὶ κατακρύπτων ἤισκε,
δέκτῃ, ὃς οὐδὲν τοῖος ἔην ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
allōi d’ auton phōti katakryptōn ēiske,
dektēi, hos ouden toios eēn epi nēusin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and as another man, concealing himself, he made himself seem,
a beggar, who was nothing such among the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: He disguised himself and made himself look like someone else, a beggar, quite unlike what he really was among the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἤισκε is the augmented imperfect of (ἐ)ίσκω ’make like, liken’ — the η- is the augment on an original ε-, not a separate long vowel, and is easy to mistake for an unaugmented form. δέκτης, ’beggar, one who receives’, is from δέχομαι.

sentences.t:
τῷ ἴκελος κατέδυ Τρώων πόλιν, οἱ δ’ ἀβάκησαν
πάντες·
sentences.tr:
tōi ikelos katedy Trōōn polin, hoi d’ abakēsan
pantes·
sentences.l:
Like to him he went down into the city of the Trojans, and they
were all astonished;
sentences.i: Looking just like that beggar, he made his way into the city of the Trojans, and everyone was astonished;
sentences.n: κατέδυ repeats the augmented aorist of 246. ἀβάκησαν, by contrast, is unaugmented: its ἀ- belongs to the verb’s own stem (privative ἀ- + the root of βάζω ’speak’, literally ’were struck speechless’), not a dropped temporal augment — Attic would lengthen a true augment here to η-.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δέ μιν οἴη ἀνέγνων τοῖον ἐόντα,
καί μιν ἀνηρώτων·
sentences.tr:
egō de min oiē anegnōn toion eonta,
kai min anērōtōn·
sentences.l:
but I alone recognized him, being such as he was,
and I questioned him;
sentences.i: but I alone recognized him for what he really was, and questioned him;
sentences.n: ἀνέγνων (ἀνα-έγνων) and ἀνηρώτων (ἀνα-ἠρώτων) are both augmented — the augments ἐ- and ἠ- are fused inside the tmesis compounds and easy to overlook. οἴη, ’alone’ (feminine), marks that only Helen, of all the Trojans, saw through Odysseus’s disguise.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ κερδοσύνῃ ἀλέεινεν.
sentences.tr: ho de kerdosynēi aleeinen.
sentences.l: but he by his craftiness evaded me.
sentences.i: but with his native cunning he evaded me.
sentences.n: ἀλέεινεν is unaugmented (from ἀλεείνω ’avoid, shun’; Attic would lengthen the initial α- to η- under the augment). κερδοσύνη, ’craftiness, cunning’, is built on the same root as κέρδεα οἶδεν, already used of Odysseus’s stock cleverness.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή μιν ἐγὼ λόεον καὶ χρῖον ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δὲ εἵματα ἕσσα καὶ ὤμοσα καρτερὸν ὅρκον
μὴ μὲν πρὶν Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ Τρώεσσ’ ἀναφῆναι,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē min egō loeon kai chrion elaiōi,
amphi de heimata hessa kai ōmosa karteron horkon
mē men prin Odysēa meta Trōess’ anaphēnai,
sentences.l:
But when I bathed him, and anointed him with oil,
and put garments about him, and swore a mighty oath
not to reveal Odysseus among the Trojans,
sentences.i: But when I had bathed him, anointed him with oil, and put clothes on him, and had sworn a solemn oath not to reveal that this was Odysseus among the Trojans,
sentences.n: λόεον and χρῖον are unaugmented imperfects (λόω ’wash’, χρίω ’anoint’); ἕσσα is the unaugmented aorist of ἕννυμι ’clothe’; ὤμοσα is the augmented first-person aorist of ὄμνυμι ’swear’. The correlative μὴ… πρίν… πρίν γε, ’not… before… until’, is split across the unit boundary here, forced by the four-line cap, and is completed in the next unit.

sentences.t:
πρίν γε τὸν ἐς νῆάς τε θοὰς κλισίας τ’ ἀφικέσθαι,
καὶ τότε δή μοι πάντα νόον κατέλεξεν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
prin ge ton es nēas te thoas klisias t’ aphikesthai,
kai tote dē moi panta noon katelexen Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
not until he had reached the swift ships and the huts,
then at last he told me all the plan of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: not until he had reached the swift ships and the huts, only then did he tell me the whole plan of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἀφικέσθαι completes the πρίν γε clause begun in the previous unit. κατέλεξεν, ’recounted, told in order’, is the same verb Helen used of her own coming narration at 239 (καταλέξω): the disguised beggar and the storytelling queen are both, in this passage, tellers of ἐοικότα.

sentences.t:
πολλοὺς δὲ Τρώων κτείνας ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ
ἦλθε μετ’ Ἀργείους, κατὰ δὲ φρόνιν ἤγαγε πολλήν.
sentences.tr:
pollous de Trōōn kteinas tanaēkeï chalkōi
ēlthe met’ Argeious, kata de phronin ēgage pollēn.
sentences.l:
And many of the Trojans having killed with long-edged bronze,
he came back among the Argives, and brought back much knowledge.
sentences.i: And after killing many Trojans with the long-edged bronze, he made his way back to the Argives, bringing back a great deal of intelligence.
sentences.n: φρόνις, ’knowledge, intelligence’ (built on the root of φρήν), is a rare noun found only here in Homer and is kept plain rather than folded into any already-fixed φρήν-compound. ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ, ’with the long-edged bronze’, combines ταναός ’long, stretched’ with ἀκή ’point, edge’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἄλλαι Τρῳαὶ λίγ’ ἐκώκυον·
sentences.tr: enth’ allai Trōiai lig’ ekōkyon·
sentences.l: Then the other Trojan women wailed shrilly;
sentences.i: Then the other Trojan women raised a shrill wail;
sentences.n: ἐκώκυον IS augmented: κωκύω begins with a consonant, so its imperfect takes the ordinary prefixed syllabic augment ἐ- (unaugmented would be the bare κώκυον), the verb specifically for a woman’s shrill ritual wail, distinct from ordinary weeping. The other Trojan women’s grief here is set directly against Helen’s private relief in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὸν κῆρ
χαῖρ’, ἐπεὶ ἤδη μοι κραδίη τέτραπτο νέεσθαι
ἂψ οἶκόνδ’, ἄτην δὲ μετέστενον, ἣν Ἀφροδίτη
δῶχ’, ὅτε μ’ ἤγαγε κεῖσε φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης,
sentences.tr:
autar emon kēr
chair’, epei ēdē moi kradiē tetrapto neesthai
aps oikond’, atēn de metestenon, hēn Aphroditē
dōch’, hote m’ ēgage keise philēs apo patridos aiēs,
sentences.l:
but my heart
rejoiced, since already my spirit had turned to return
back home, and I mourned over the blindness which Aphrodite
gave, when she led me there, away from my dear fatherland,
sentences.i: but my own heart rejoiced, since by then my spirit had turned toward returning home again, and I lamented the blindness that Aphrodite had given me, when she led me there, away from my dear fatherland,
sentences.n: τέτραπτο is a pluperfect passive of τρέπω, ’had been turned’; κραδίη and κῆρ, both simply ’heart’, stand one right after the other for two different Homeric words for the same organ. ἄτη is the ruinous blindness or delusion a god sends, here laid at Aphrodite’s door as the cause of Helen’s abduction; δῶχ’ is δῶκε, an unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι.

sentences.t:
παῖδά τ’ ἐμὴν νοσφισσαμένην θάλαμόν τε πόσιν τε
οὔ τευ δευόμενον, οὔτ’ ἂρ φρένας οὔτε τι εἶδος.
sentences.tr:
paida t’ emēn nosphissamenēn thalamon te posin te
ou teu deuomenon, out’ ar phrenas oute ti eidos.
sentences.l:
forsaking my daughter, and my chamber, and my husband,
a man lacking in nothing, neither in mind nor at all in looks.”
sentences.i: abandoning my daughter, my marriage chamber, and my husband — a man who lacked nothing, neither in understanding nor in looks.”
sentences.n: νοσφισσαμένην is an aorist middle participle, ’having forsaken, parted from’, agreeing with the speaker’s own remembered self. δευόμενον, ’lacking’, takes the genitive τευ (= τινός); φρένας is an accusative of respect. This closes Helen’s speech, opened with a quotation mark at 235: the reply-formula at 4.265 that follows (τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος) is plain narration and carries no quotation mark of its own, matching the pattern used throughout for reply-formula lines.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: In answer fair-haired Menelaus said to her:
sentences.n: This is the fixed reply-formula τὴν/τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη (house table), already used at 4.147 for this same exchange and reused here verbatim, since the wording is fixed once ratified. τήν is the pronoun ’her’, object of προσέφη, referring to Helen. ξανθός, ’fair-haired’, is Menelaus’s standing epithet. This line is pure narration: it closes Helen’s speech, open since 4.235, and makes way for Menelaus’s own words, which begin only in the next unit — so both the opening and the closing quotation marks belong there, not here.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα, γύναι, κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: nai dē tauta ge panta, gynai, kata moiran eeipes.
sentences.l: “Yes, indeed, all this, at least, wife, according to what is fitting you have spoken.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, wife, all this you have said, as is fitting.
sentences.n: Μενέλαος now answers Helen directly; her own speech has already closed on its own last unit at 4.264, and the reply-formula at 4.265 carries no quotation mark of its own, so this unit opens cleanly with Menelaus’s first word. κατὰ μοῖραν, ’according to what is fitting’ (house table), is a stock phrase of approval. γε is a limiting particle, ’at least, in fact’; δή adds emphasis, ’indeed’. ἔειπες is an augmented aorist of εἶπον (ἔ-ειπες), ’you spoke’ — contrast the several unaugmented aorists soon to follow (ἴδον, ἔσκε), unlike ἔτλη below, which is augmented despite looking similar. γύναι, vocative of γυνή, is Menelaus’s address to his wife.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν πολέων ἐδάην βουλήν τε νόον τε
ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων, πολλὴν δ’ ἐπελήλυθα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
ēdē men poleōn edaēn boulēn te noon te
andrōn hērōōn, pollēn d’ epelēlytha gaian·
sentences.l:
Already, indeed, of many I have learned the counsel and the mind
of hero-men, and much land have I traveled over;
sentences.i: By now I have learned the counsel and the mind of many heroic men, and I have traveled over much land;
sentences.n: ἐδάην is an augmented aorist passive/deponent of the root δα- ’learn’ (cf. δαῆναι), ’I have learned’ — despite its look, the initial ἐ- here is a real augment, like the several other augmented forms in Menelaus’s speech, and unlike the genuinely unaugmented ἴδον and ἔσκε just below. πολέων is the uncontracted genitive plural of πολύς (Attic πολλῶν). ἐπελήλυθα is a perfect of ἐπέρχομαι, ’I have come over, traversed’, governing γαῖαν. ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων, ’of hero-men’, is a general description, distinct from the fixed title ἥρως used with a name.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ πω τοιοῦτον ἐγὼν ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
οἷον Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος ἔσκε φίλον κῆρ.
sentences.tr:
all’ ou pō toiouton egōn idon ophthalmoisin,
hoion Odyssēos talasiphronos eske philon kēr.
sentences.l:
But never yet such a thing did I see with my eyes,
as was the dear heart of Odysseus the enduring-minded.
sentences.i: But I have never yet seen such a thing with my own eyes as the dear heart of steadfast Odysseus was.
sentences.n: ἴδον is an unaugmented aorist from the root ἰδ- (Attic εἶδον) — genuinely without an augment, unlike ἐδάην just above. ἔσκε is an unaugmented iterative imperfect of εἰμί, ’used to be, was’, marking a remembered, habitual state. φίλον κῆρ, ’his own dear heart’, is an accusative of respect. ταλασίφρων keeps the fixed house rendering, ’enduring-minded’ / ’steadfast’, already used of Odysseus earlier in this part and built on τλῆναι ’endure’ — the same root that gives ἔτλη two lines later.

sentences.t:
οἷον καὶ τόδ’ ἔρεξε καὶ ἔτλη καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ
ἵππῳ ἔνι ξεστῷ, ἵν’ ἐνήμεθα πάντες ἄριστοι
Ἀργείων Τρώεσσι φόνον καὶ κῆρα φέροντες.
sentences.tr:
hoion kai tod’ erexe kai etlē karteros anēr
hippōi eni xestōi, hin’ enēmetha pantes aristoi
Argeiōn Trōessi phonon kai kēra pherontes.
sentences.l:
Such a thing, too, this he did, and endured, the mighty man,
in the horse of polished wood, where we all sat, the best
of the Argives, bringing to the Trojans slaughter and doom.
sentences.i: That too was a thing the mighty man did and endured, inside the horse of polished wood, where all of us, the best of the Argives, sat bringing slaughter and doom to the Trojans.
sentences.n: ἔρεξε is an augmented aorist of ῥέζω ’do, perform’ (root ῥεζ-, augment ἐ-); ἔτλη is likewise augmented, a root aorist of τλῆναι ’endure’ (bare root τλη-, seen without augment in the infinitive τλῆναι), built like ἔβη and ἔστη. ξεστός means ’smoothed, planed’, of worked wood, describing the Trojan horse’s construction. Ἀργείων is one of Homer’s three names for the Greeks, alongside Ἀχαιοί and Δαναοί. φόνον καὶ κῆρα, ’slaughter and doom’, is a doublet; the phrase τόδ’ ἔρεξε καὶ ἔτλη καρτερὸς ἀνήρ echoes Helen’s own account of the same feat a few lines earlier.

sentences.t:
ἦλθες ἔπειτα σὺ κεῖσε· κελευσέμεναι δέ σ’ ἔμελλε
δαίμων, ὃς Τρώεσσιν ἐβούλετο κῦδος ὀρέξαι·
sentences.tr:
ēlthes epeita sy keise· keleusemenai de s’ emelle
daimōn, hos Trōessin ebouleto kydos orexai·
sentences.l:
You came then yourself to that place; and to urge you on was destined
a god, who wished to grant glory to the Trojans;
sentences.i: Then you came there yourself, and a god was destined to urge you on, one who wished to grant glory to the Trojans;
sentences.n: κεῖσε, ’to that place, thither’, is a directional adverb, an old formation distinct from the -θεν/-θι/-δε suffixes seen elsewhere. σύ is emphatic here, ’you yourself’. ἔμελλε + infinitive is ’was destined, was about to’. δαίμων is left deliberately vague, ’a god, some divine power’, unnamed — Menelaus does not say which one. ὀρέξαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀρέγω ’stretch out, offer, grant’, governing κῦδος ’glory’.

sentences.t: καί τοι Δηΐφοβος θεοείκελος ἕσπετ’ ἰούσῃ.
sentences.tr: kai toi Dēïphobos theoeikelos hespet’ iousēi.
sentences.l: And god-resembling Deiphobus followed you as you went.
sentences.i: and Deiphobus, who was like a god, went along with you as you went.
sentences.n: τοι here is the enclitic dative pronoun ’to/for you’ (not the affirming particle τοι), object of ἕσπετ(ο) ’followed, accompanied’ (aorist of ἕπομαι + dat.); ἰούσῃ, a dative feminine participle of εἶμι, agrees with the same ’you’ and specifies ’as you were going’. θεοείκελος, ’god-resembling’, is the epithet already fixed for Telemachus at 3.416 (’who was like a god’); here it is applied to a new referent, Deiphobus, a son of Priam and a leading Trojan warrior.

sentences.t:
τρὶς δὲ περίστειξας κοῖλον λόχον ἀμφαφόωσα,
ἐκ δ’ ὀνομακλήδην Δαναῶν ὀνόμαζες ἀρίστους,
πάντων Ἀργείων φωνὴν ἴσκουσ’ ἀλόχοισιν.
sentences.tr:
tris de peristeixas koilon lochon amphaphoōsa,
ek d’ onomaklēdēn Danaōn onomazes aristous,
pantōn Argeiōn phōnēn iskous’ alochoisin.
sentences.l:
And three times around you walked, the hollow ambush touching all over,
and by name you called out the best of the Danaans,
to all the Argives’ wives your voice making like.
sentences.i: Three times you walked around the hollow ambush, feeling it all over, and called out the best of the Danaans each by name, making your voice like that of every one of the Argives’ wives.
sentences.n: κοῖλον λόχον, ’the hollow ambush’, names the horse’s inside as the place of hiding, transferring λόχος (properly ’a body of men lying in wait’) to the vessel that concealed them. ἀμφαφόωσα is an uncontracted present participle of ἀμφαφάω, ’feel, touch all over’, with the vowel stretched (diectasis) as at 1.32. ὀνομακλήδην, ’calling by name’, is an adverb formed on ὄνομα. ἴσκουσα, from ἴσκω ’liken, make resemble’, takes φωνήν as an internal accusative and ἀλόχοισιν as the dative of comparison, ’like to the wives’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ καὶ Τυδεΐδης καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἥμενοι ἐν μέσσοισιν ἀκούσαμεν ὡς ἐβόησας.
sentences.tr:
autar egō kai Tydeïdēs kai dios Odysseus
hēmenoi en messoisin akousamen hōs eboēsas.
sentences.l:
But I, and the son of Tydeus, and heavenly Odysseus,
sitting in the middle, heard how you cried out.
sentences.i: But I, and the son of Tydeus, and heavenly Odysseus, sitting in the midst, heard how you cried out.
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδης keeps the fixed periphrasis ’the son of Tydeus’ for Diomedes; δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς keeps the fixed ’heavenly’ reserved for this epithet of Odysseus. ἀκούσαμεν is an unaugmented aorist of ἀκούω (Attic would show the augment as ἠκούσαμεν, with η- from ἐ+ἀ), unlike the ordinary augmented ἐβόησας just after it in the same line — a reminder that augmented and unaugmented forms sit side by side even within one sentence. ἥμενοι is the present participle of ἧμαι ’sit’.

sentences.t:
νῶι μὲν ἀμφοτέρω μενεήναμεν ὁρμηθέντε
ἢ ἐξελθέμεναι, ἢ ἔνδοθεν αἶψ’ ὑπακοῦσαι·
sentences.tr:
nōi men amphoterō meneēnamen hormēthente
ē exelthemenai, ē endothen aips’ hypakousai·
sentences.l:
We two, both of us, were eager, having started up,
either to go out, or from within quickly to answer;
sentences.i: The two of us were eager, both starting up, either to go outside or to answer quickly from within;
sentences.n: νῶι ... ἀμφοτέρω doubles the dual pronoun with ’both’ for emphasis, ’the two of us, both together’. μενεήναμεν is an unaugmented aorist of μενεαίνω ’be eager, strain towards’ (the expected augmented form would be ἐμενεήναμεν) — a different sense of the verb from μενέαινεν ’raged’ used of Poseidon at 1.20. ὁρμηθέντε is the dual aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω ’set in motion’. ἐξελθέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic ἐξελθεῖν); ὑπακοῦσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὑπακούω ’listen and respond’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κατέρυκε καὶ ἔσχεθεν ἱεμένω περ.
sentences.tr: all’ Odyseus kateryke kai eschethen hiemenō per.
sentences.l: But Odysseus held us back, and restrained us, eager though we were.
sentences.i: But Odysseus held us back and checked us, eager as we were.
sentences.n: κατέρυκε is the unaugmented imperfect already glossed for this verb (Attic κατήρυκε), ’was holding back, tried to restrain’. ἔσχεθεν is a third-singular aorist of ἔχω with the epic by-form ending -θε, here with the movable -ν added before the following vowel of ἱεμένω — not a dual or plural form, despite its look, since the subject remains the singular Ὀδυσεύς. ἱεμένω is the dual participle of ἵεμαι ’be eager, strain forward’, with concessive περ, ’though eager’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἀκὴν ἔσαν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
Ἄντικλος δὲ σέ γ’ οἶος ἀμείψασθαι ἐπέεσσιν
ἤθελεν.
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi men pantes akēn esan huies Achaiōn,
Antiklos de se g’ oios ameipsasthai epeessin
ēthelen.
sentences.l:
Then all the other sons of the Achaeans were silent,
but Antiklos alone wished you, at least, to answer
with words.
sentences.i: Then all the other sons of the Achaeans were silent, but Antiklos alone wanted to answer you with words.
sentences.n: ἀκήν, ’silently, in silence’, is an adverb found only here in this part. υἷες Ἀχαιῶν keeps the fixed periphrasis ’sons of the Achaeans’. Ἄντικλος is a proper name that occurs nowhere else in the poem, so it carries no fixed epithet and is rendered plainly, ’Antiklos’. σέ γε, ’you, at least’, is the emphatic object of ἀμείψασθαι ’to answer’ (aorist middle infinitive of ἀμείβομαι), governed by ἤθελεν, ’he wished’, which spills over into the next line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἐπὶ μάστακα χερσὶ πίεζεν
νωλεμέως κρατερῇσι, σάωσε δὲ πάντας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr:
all’ Odyseus epi mastaka chersi piezen
nōlemeōs kraterēisi, saōse de pantas Achaious·
sentences.l:
But Odysseus upon his mouth with his hands pressed down,
unrelentingly, with his strong hands, and saved all the Achaeans;
sentences.i: But Odysseus pressed his hands hard over his mouth, without relenting, and so saved all the Achaeans;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ ... πίεζεν is tmesis for ἐπίεζεν, ’pressed down upon, throttled’, with μάστακα, a poetic word for ’mouth’ (root of μασάομαι ’chew’), as its object. χερσὶ ... κρατερῇσι, ’with strong hands’, is split across the two lines by hyperbaton. νωλεμέως, ’without a break, relentlessly’, intensifies the grip. σάωσε is an unaugmented aorist of σαόω (Attic σῴζω) ’save’. Antiklos alone wanted to break the silence and answer Helen’s mimicked voices; Odysseus’s grip on his mouth kept the whole company from betraying itself.

sentences.t: τόφρα δ’ ἔχ’, ὄφρα σε νόσφιν ἀπήγαγε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: tophra d’ ech’, ophra se nosphin apēgage Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: And so long he held on, until apart Pallas Athena led you away.”
sentences.i: and he kept holding on that long, until Pallas Athena led you off apart.”
sentences.n: τόφρα ... ὄφρα is a correlative pair, ’so long ... until’, with ὄφρα here temporal rather than final, taking the indicative ἀπήγαγε for a definite past event. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω (’held’; the Attic imperfect εἶχε shows the same augment fused into the stem), continuing the grip of κατέρυκε and πίεζεν above. νόσφιν, ’apart, away’, matches its use at 1.19. This closes Menelaus’s whole account of the wooden horse, and with it his speech; the closing quotation mark belongs here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The fixed fourth reply-formula (house table), used throughout this part for Telemachus’s replies (cf. 4.156, 4.316). τόν, ’him’, refers to Menelaus; πεπνυμένος, ’prudent’, is Telemachus’s standing epithet. As with 4.265, this is pure narration between the two speeches — Menelaus’s has just closed, and Telemachus’s opens only in the next unit, which therefore alone carries the mark and the opening quotation mark.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
ἄλγιον· οὐ γάρ οἵ τι τάδ’ ἤρκεσε λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον,
οὐδ’ εἴ οἱ κραδίη γε σιδηρέη ἔνδοθεν ἦεν.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē Menelae diotrephes, orchame laōn,
algion· ou gar hoi ti tad’ ērkese lygron olethron,
oud’ ei hoi kradiē ge sidēreē endothen ēen.
sentences.l:
“Atreus' son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
all the more painful; for not at all did this ward off from him grievous destruction,
not even if his heart, at least, had been iron within.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, it is all the more painful, for none of this warded off grievous destruction from him, not even if his heart within had been iron.
sentences.n: Line 291 repeats verbatim the vocative address already fixed for Peisistratus’s replies to Menelaus (4.156, 4.316); the same wording stands here for Telemachus. ἄλγιον, a comparative adverb of ἄλγος ’pain’ used absolutely, means ’an added grief, all the more painful’. ἤρκεσε, from ἀρκέω ’be enough to ward off’, takes an accusative of the danger (τάδ’) and a dative of the person (οἵ, ’for him’, referring to Odysseus): ’none of this warded off grievous destruction for him’. σιδηρέη ... ἔνδοθεν, ’of iron within’, is a stock image for an unbreakable will.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ εἰς εὐνὴν τράπεθ’ ἡμέας, ὄφρα καὶ ἤδη
ὕπνῳ ὕπο γλυκερῷ ταρπώμεθα κοιμηθέντες.
sentences.tr:
all’ aget’ eis eunēn trapeth’ hēmeas, ophra kai ēdē
hypnōi hypo glykerōi tarpōmetha koimēthentes.
sentences.l:
But come, turn us to our bed, so that now indeed
with sweet sleep we may take our fill, having lain down to rest.”
sentences.i: But come, send us to bed, so that we may now at last take our fill of sweet sleep, once we have lain down.”
sentences.n: ἄγετ(ε), a plural imperative, ’come now!’, is addressed generally to the household as much as to Menelaus. τράπεθ’ = τράπετε, an aorist imperative of τρέπω ’turn’, here ’send (us) to’. ταρπώμεθα is an aorist subjunctive of τέρπομαι ’take one’s fill of, enjoy’, governing the dative ὕπνῳ γλυκερῷ ’sweet sleep’; κοιμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of κοιμάω, ’having lain down’. This closes Telemachus’s short, grief-toned reply, and the closing quotation mark belongs here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀργείη δ’ Ἑλένη δμῳῇσι κέλευσεν
δέμνι’ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ θέμεναι καὶ ῥήγεα καλὰ
πορφύρε’ ἐμβαλέειν στορέσαι τ’ ἐφύπερθε τάπητας,
χλαίνας τ’ ἐνθέμεναι οὔλας καθύπερθεν ἕσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, Argeiē d’ Helenē dmōiēisi keleusen
demni’ hyp’ aithousēi themenai kai rhēgea kala
porphyre’ embaleein storesai t’ ephyperthe tapētas,
chlainas t’ enthemenai oulas kathyperthen hesasthai.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Argive Helen gave the handmaids orders
to place bedsteads under the portico, and fine blankets,
purple, to throw on, and to spread carpets over them,
and to put in thick cloaks, to wear as covering on top.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Argive Helen ordered her handmaids to place bedsteads under the portico, throw fine purple blankets on them, spread carpets over the top, and put in thick cloaks to serve as covering on top.
sentences.n: δμῳῇσι, dative plural, are the household’s slave-women, given the standard hospitality task of making up a guest’s bed: bedsteads (δέμνια) set under the portico (αἴθουσα, already fixed as ’the portico’, cf. 3.399), fine purple rugs (ῥήγεα πορφύρεα) thrown on, carpets (τάπητας) spread over them, and thick cloaks (χλαῖναι) laid in to serve as covering on top. Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, ’Argive Helen’, is her name-formula without the added Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα used at 4.184.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἴσαν ἐκ μεγάροιο δάος μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαι,
δέμνια δὲ στόρεσαν·
sentences.tr:
hai d’ isan ek megaroio daos meta chersin echousai,
demnia de storesan·
sentences.l:
And they went out of the hall, torches in their hands holding,
and the bedsteads they spread;
sentences.i: And they went out of the hall, holding torches in their hands, and made up the beds;
sentences.n: αἱ, feminine plural pronoun ’they’, picks up the δμῳαί just given their orders. δάος is a rare old form for ’torch(es)’ (usually δαΐς, δαΐδα), here probably a collective, related to δαίω ’kindle’. στόρεσαν is an unaugmented aorist of στόρνυμι ’spread’ (cf. στορέσαι just above), continuing the list of bed-making tasks Helen has just ordered.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ ξείνους ἄγε κῆρυξ.
sentences.tr: ek de xeinous age kēryx.
sentences.l: and out the guests the herald led.
sentences.i: and the herald led the guests out.
sentences.n: This clause names a separate subject and action from the maids’ bed-making just described, so it is kept as its own sense-unit rather than folded into the previous one. ἄγε is an unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω ’lead’ (Attic ἦγε, with the augment fused into the diphthong); the tense frames the leading-out as ongoing alongside the maids’ work. κῆρυξ, ’the herald’, appears without further description, his standing role in this house already established.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐν προδόμῳ δόμου αὐτόθι κοιμήσαντο,
Τηλέμαχός θ’ ἥρως καὶ Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr:
hoi men ar’ en prodomōi domou autothi koimēsanto,
Tēlemachos th’ hērōs kai Nestoros aglaos huios·
sentences.l:
So then they lay down to sleep there in the forecourt of the house,
both the hero Telemachus and Nestor's splendid son;
sentences.i: So they lay down to sleep right there in the forecourt of the house, Telemachus the hero and Nestor's splendid son;
sentences.n: πρόδομος, ’the forecourt’, is the space just inside a house’s entrance, distinct from the outer αἴθουσα and πρόθυρον already met in Book 3. κοιμήσαντο is an unaugmented aorist middle of κοιμάω ’lie down to sleep’, echoing κοιμηθέντες in Telemachus’s own words just above. The line Τηλέμαχός θ’ ἥρως καὶ Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱός repeats, word for word, a line already published for this same pair of guests, and keeps its established English.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ καθεῦδε μυχῷ δόμου ὑψηλοῖο,
πὰρ δ’ Ἑλένη τανύπεπλος ἐλέξατο, δῖα γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdēs de katheude mychōi domou hypsēloio,
par d’ Helenē tanypeplos elexato, dia gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
And the son of Atreus slept in the recess of the high house,
and beside him lay long-robed Helen, heavenly-one of women.
sentences.i: And the son of Atreus slept in the innermost recess of the high house, and beside him lay long-robed Helen, heavenly among women.
sentences.n: μυχός, ’the innermost recess’, names the private inner chamber of the house, as opposed to the guests’ portico. δόμου ὑψηλοῖο repeats the fixed ’the high house’ (cf. 3.402). τανύπεπλος, ’long-robed’ (τανύ- ’long, stretched’ + πέπλος ’robe’), is fixed here as Helen’s standing epithet, since it is likely to recur. δῖα γυναικῶν repeats the formula already fixed for Penelope, ’heavenly-one of women’ / ’heavenly among women’, now given to Helen with the identical wording, since Homer uses the same phrase of both.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
ὤρνυτ’ ἄρ’ ἐξ εὐνῆφι βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
εἵματα ἑσσάμενος, περὶ δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ θέτ’ ὤμῳ,
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
ōrnyt’ ar’ ex eunēphi boēn agathos Menelaos
heimata hessamenos, peri de xiphos oxy thet’ ōmōi,
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
up rose from his bed good at the war-cry Menelaus,
his clothes having put on, and round, a sharp sword he set on his shoulder,
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, up rose from his bed Menelaus, good at the war-cry, and he put on his clothes and slung a sharp sword about his shoulder,
sentences.n: This whole three-line passage repeats, almost word for word, the formulaic dawn-and-arming lines already shipped in odyssey-005 (2.1–3), where the subject was Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός ’Odysseus’ dear son’; here only the subject changes, to βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος, the house-fixed epithet ’good at the war-cry’. ὤρνυτ’ is ὤρνυτο, an AUGMENTED imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ’rise’ (root ὀρ-νυ-; the temporal augment lengthens ο to ω, as in ὀφείλω beside ὤφειλον), not an aorist. ἑσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἕννυμι ’clothe’; περὶ … θέτ’ is tmesis for περιέθετο. εὐνῆφι carries the old case-suffix -φι, ablatival, ’from his bed’.

sentences.t:
ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο θεῷ ἐναλίγκιος ἄντην,
Τηλεμάχῳ δὲ παρῖζεν, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr:
possi d’ hypo liparoisin edēsato kala pedila,
bē d’ imen ek thalamoio theōi enalinkios antēn,
Tēlemachōi de parizen, epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l:
and under his sleek feet he bound fine sandals,
and set out to go from the chamber, like to a god to look upon,
and beside Telemachus he sat, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: he bound fine sandals beneath his sleek feet, went out of his chamber like a god to look upon, sat down beside Telemachus, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: Lines 309–310 reuse, unchanged, the couplet already shipped word for word in odyssey-005 (2.4–5), there too of a man arming at dawn; there it closed the sentence with a full stop, but here the sentence runs on into 311, so the same Greek carries a comma instead. ἐδήσατο is an AUGMENTED aorist middle, like ὤρνυτ’ just above; ὑπὸ … ἐδήσατο is tmesis. παρῖζεν is an imperfect of παρίζω, its augment hidden inside the long ῑ. The closing phrase ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν matches the house table’s fixed rendering of this address-formula (’spoke a word, and called him by name’).

sentences.t:
τίπτε δέ σε χρειὼ δεῦρ’ ἤγαγε, Τηλέμαχ’ ἥρως,
ἐς Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν, ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης;
sentences.tr:
tipte de se chreiō deur’ ēgage, Tēlemach’ hērōs,
es Lakedaimona dian, ep’ eurea nōta thalassēs;
sentences.l:
“Why then has need brought you here, Telemachus, hero,
to heavenly Lacedaemon, over the broad back of the sea?
sentences.i: “Why has necessity brought you here, hero Telemachus, to heavenly Lacedaemon, over the broad back of the sea?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε contracted, ’why ever’. χρειώ ’need, necessity’ is treated as the grammatical agent of ἤγαγε, an AUGMENTED aorist of ἄγω (ἠ- from ἀ-). ἥρως, vocative in direct address to Telemachus, is the house-fixed title ’the hero’ (already used generically), here simply ’hero’. Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν is the house-fixed ’heavenly Lacedaemon’. νῶτα θαλάσσης, ’the back(s) of the sea’, uses the poetic plural νῶτα for a single stretch of open water. This opens Menelaus’s question and Murray’s next paragraph.

sentences.t: δήμιον ἦ ἴδιον;
sentences.tr: dēmion ē idion;
sentences.l: Public, or private?
sentences.i: Is this a public matter, or a private one?
sentences.n: δήμιον and ἴδιον are neuter adjectives standing for an unspoken noun (something like πρῆγμα ’matter, business’), each agreeing with it in turn; the same antithesis, ’private, not public’, was Telemachus’s own description of his errand to Nestor at 3.82 (odyssey-009: πρῆξις δ’ ἥδ’ ἰδίη, οὐ δήμιος), and Menelaus now puts it to him as a question. ἦ here is the disjunctive interrogative particle ’or’, to be told apart from asseverative ἦ ’truly’ and from ἦ ’(he/she) spoke’.

sentences.t: τόδε μοι νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες.
sentences.tr: tode moi nēmertes enispes.
sentences.l: tell me this, the unerring truth.”
sentences.i: tell me the unerring truth of it.”
sentences.n: ἐνίσπες is an aorist imperative of the defective verb ἐνέπω/ἐνίσπω ’tell, declare’, the same verb as ἔννεπε at 1.1. With νημερτές ’unerring’ (νη- + the root of ἁμαρτάνω ’miss the mark’) it forms the recurring idiom ’tell me the unerring truth’, heard again in Telemachus’s own mouth at the very end of this part (331). τόδε ’this’ picks up the alternative just posed. The closing ” falls here: Menelaus’s question, opened at 312, is now complete, and Telemachus answers next.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This whole line is the house-fixed reply-formula for Telemachus (already shipped three times, with τόν, in odyssey-004), reused here unchanged; πεπνυμένος ’prudent’ is his standing epithet throughout the poem. Plain narration, no speech-mark of its own: it only introduces the words that follow. It also opens Murray’s next paragraph, the last of this part.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
ἤλυθον, εἴ τινά μοι κληηδόνα πατρὸς ἐνίσποις.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē Menelae diotrephes, orchame laōn,
ēlython, ei tina moi klēēdona patros enispois.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’ son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
I have come, in case some tidings of my father you might tell me.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, I have come, in the hope that you might tell me some news of my father.
sentences.n: The vocative line reuses the house-fixed rendering already shipped for this same address (also used by Telemachus of Menelaus earlier in this part, at line 291). ἤλυθον is an AUGMENTED aorist (= Attic ἦλθον; the epic form keeps the same lengthened η, root ἐλθ-/ἐλυθ-, adding only an epenthetic -υ-), not an unaugmented form. κληηδών is the Ionic by-form of κληδών ’report, rumor’ (root of κλέος, κλύω). ἐνίσποις, an aorist optative of the same defective verb seen as an imperative at 314, with εἴ makes a wishful condition, ’in case you might tell’. This opens Telemachus’s own plea, left running to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
ἐσθίεταί μοι οἶκος, ὄλωλε δὲ πίονα ἔργα,
δυσμενέων δ’ ἀνδρῶν πλεῖος δόμος, οἵ τέ μοι αἰεὶ
μῆλ’ ἁδινὰ σφάζουσι καὶ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς,
μητρὸς ἐμῆς μνηστῆρες ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν ἔχοντες.
sentences.tr:
esthietai moi oikos, olōle de piona erga,
dysmeneōn d’ andrōn pleios domos, hoi te moi aiei
mēl’ hadina sphazousi kai eilipodas helikas bous,
mētros emēs mnēstēres hyperbion hybrin echontes.
sentences.l:
My house is being eaten up, and my rich estate is ruined,
and of hostile men the house is full, who for me always
thronging sheep slaughter, and rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle,
suitors of my mother, having overweening insolence.
sentences.i: My house is being eaten up, and my rich estate is ruined; the house is full of hostile men, who are always slaughtering my thronging sheep and the cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn — suitors of my mother, with their overbearing insolence.
sentences.n: ἐσθίεταί is present passive, a vivid ’is being eaten up’ even now; ὄλωλε is the perfect of ὄλλυμι, ’stands ruined’. οἵ τε carries the epic τε of a standing, habitual fact. Line 320 repeats 1.92 word for word, and both μῆλ’ ἁδινά ’thronging sheep’ and εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς ’rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle’ are house-fixed renderings already shipped there, reused unchanged. Line 321 opens with words Telemachus himself already used of the suitors, addressing them directly, at 1.368 (odyssey-004): ’suitors of my mother, having overweening insolence’, reused verbatim here, now spoken of them rather than to them.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα νῦν τὰ σὰ γούναθ’ ἱκάνομαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα
κείνου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον ἐνισπεῖν, εἴ που ὄπωπας
ὀφθαλμοῖσι τεοῖσιν ἢ ἄλλου μῦθον ἄκουσας
πλαζομένου·
sentences.tr:
touneka nyn ta sa gounath’ hikanomai, ai k’ ethelēistha
keinou lygron olethron enispein, ei pou opōpas
ophthalmoisi teoisin ē allou mython akousas
plazomenou·
sentences.l:
Therefore now to your knees I come, in case you may be willing
of that man the bitter destruction to tell, if somewhere you saw it
with your own eyes, or from another heard the tale,
a wanderer;
sentences.i: That is why I have come now to your knees, in the hope that you may be willing to tell me of his bitter destruction, if you perhaps saw it with your own eyes, or heard the tale from some other wanderer;
sentences.n: These four lines reuse, word for word, the wording already shipped for the identical Greek at 3.92–95 (odyssey-009), where Telemachus made the same plea to Nestor: Homer has him repeat it almost verbatim to a second host. Coming to a man’s knees is the suppliant’s gesture. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα uses the old 2nd-person subjunctive ending -σθα. ἄκουσας is UNAUGMENTED (Attic ἤκουσας), taking the genitive ἄλλου. πλαζομένου, ’wandering’, agrees with ἄλλου, ’some other wanderer’.

sentences.t: περὶ γάρ μιν ὀιζυρὸν τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.tr: peri gar min oizyron teke mētēr.
sentences.l: for beyond all others his mother bore him to misery.
sentences.i: for his mother bore him to more misery than any other man.
sentences.n: This clause reuses, unchanged, the English already shipped for the same recurring Greek formula at 3.95 (odyssey-009), the tail end of the same repeated plea. περί, with the accent thrown back in Homer’s usual practice (though printed περί rather than πέρι here), is the adverb ’beyond all, exceedingly’. μιν is Odysseus; τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω (Attic ἔτεκε), ’bore’.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τί μ’ αἰδόμενος μειλίσσεο μηδ’ ἐλεαίρων,
ἀλλ’ εὖ μοι κατάλεξον ὅπως ἤντησας ὀπωπῆς.
sentences.tr:
mēde ti m’ aidomenos meilisseo mēd’ eleairōn,
all’ eu moi katalexon hopōs ēntēsas opōpēs.
sentences.l:
And do not at all, out of respect, soften things for me, nor out of pity,
but recount to me well how you came upon the sight.
sentences.i: Do not soften anything for me out of respect or pity, but tell me plainly how you came to see it.
sentences.n: This couplet again reuses, unchanged, the English already shipped for the identical Greek at 3.96–97 (odyssey-009); the second line is also a house-fixed rendering in its own right. αἰδόμενος is ’out of respect, from delicacy’ (from αἴδομαι); ἐλεαίρων is the epic by-form of ἐλεέω ’pity’. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω; ἤντησας is an AUGMENTED aorist (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-), ’you met with’, governing the genitive ὀπωπῆς ’the sight’.

sentences.t:
λίσσομαι, εἴ ποτέ τοί τι πατὴρ ἐμός, ἐσθλὸς Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἢ ἔπος ἠέ τι ἔργον ὑποστὰς ἐξετέλεσσε
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχετε πήματ’ Ἀχαιοί,
τῶν νῦν μοι μνῆσαι, καί μοι νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες.
sentences.tr:
lissomai, ei pote toi ti patēr emos, esthlos Odysseus
ē epos ēe ti ergon hypostas exetelesse
dēmōi eni Trōōn, hothi paschete pēmat’ Achaioi,
tōn nyn moi mnēsai, kai moi nēmertes enispes.
sentences.l:
I beseech you, if ever for you my father, good Odysseus,
either a word or some deed having promised, fulfilled it
in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans,
of these things now for me be mindful, and tell me the unerring truth.
sentences.i: I beseech you, if ever my father, good Odysseus, promised you some word or deed and made it good in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes, remember it now for my sake, and tell me the unerring truth.
sentences.n: This whole four-line plea reuses, word for word, the wording Telemachus used, verbatim, to Nestor at 3.98–101 (odyssey-009) — the same request repeated to a second host. λίσσομαι ’I beseech’ grounds the appeal in a past service; ὑποστάς (aor. part. of ὑφίστημι) is ’having promised’; ἐξετέλεσσε keeps its augment (ἐξ-ε-τέλεσσε) though πάσχετε beside it is unaugmented (= ἐπάσχετε). Unlike at 3.101, the speech does NOT close here: Telemachus is still speaking when this part ends, so no closing ” is given — his plea to Menelaus stays open, to be closed only when a future part (odyssey-017) resumes it, exactly as odyssey-014’s last open speech was closed only in odyssey-015.
